key_results: Compression is classified both by fidelity (lossless versus lossy) and by whether input/output group sizes are fixed or variable. Lossless methods must reconstruct every bit; lossy methods trade controlled signal degradation for much higher compression. [Chapter 27, Data Compression Strategies, Table 27-1]

Run-length encoding replaces a run by a value/flag and count; it compresses only when runs are long enough and can enlarge data dominated by isolated occurrences. PackBits generalizes the idea by using a signed count convention. [Chapter 27, Run-Length Encoding, Fig. 27-1]

Huffman coding assigns shorter prefix-free codes to more probable symbols, with ideal code length proportional to the negative logarithm of symbol probability. Proper prefix selection lets a variable-length bitstream be decoded without explicit delimiters. [Chapter 27, Huffman Encoding, Fig. 27-3]

Delta encoding stores the first sample and then successive differences. For slowly varying signals it concentrates values near zero, making subsequent Huffman or run-length coding more effective; linear predictive coding generalizes the predictor from the previous sample to several past samples. [Chapter 27, Delta Encoding, Figs. 27-4–27-5]

LZW is a lossless dictionary method that starts with single-byte codes, emits fixed-width codes for the longest known strings, and builds matching code tables during compression and decompression, so the dictionary need not be transmitted separately. [Chapter 27, LZW Compression, Figs. 27-6–27-8 and Table 27-3]

JPEG transform compression partitions an image into 8×8 blocks, applies a 2-D DCT, quantizes coefficients more aggressively at high spatial frequencies, serializes coefficients in zigzag order, run-length encodes zero runs, and finishes with Huffman or arithmetic coding. [Chapter 27, JPEG, Figs. 27-9–27-14]

The DCT is advantageous for block image compression because its lowest nonconstant basis functions contain half cycles and therefore model gradual brightness ramps more economically than the Fourier transform's full-cycle lowest frequencies. [Chapter 27, JPEG, Fig. 27-10 and printed p. 501]

MPEG combines intraframe JPEG-like compression with interframe prediction: I-pictures are independently coded, P-pictures refer to earlier frames, and B-pictures can refer to both earlier and later frames. [Chapter 27, MPEG, printed p. 502]

Real-time DSP differs from offline computation because it must sustain the input sample rate indefinitely; extra throughput costs power, money, and design effort, so the relevant requirement is a bounded cycles-per-sample budget. [Chapter 28, How DSPs Are Different from Other Microprocessors]

A real-time FIR filter maintains recent samples and coefficients in circular buffers. Each output requires interrupt handling, two circular-buffer fetch/update streams, multiply-accumulate work, and loop control; DSP hardware is arranged to execute many of these operations in parallel. [Chapter 28, Circular Buffering, Fig. 28-3 and Table 28-1]

Harvard architecture separates instruction and data memories so an instruction and data can be fetched simultaneously; Super Harvard architecture adds an instruction cache and an I/O controller, freeing buses and supporting concurrent computation and data transfer. [Chapter 28, Architecture of the Digital Signal Processor, Figs. 28-4–28-5]

DSP address generators provide zero-overhead circular and bit-reversed addressing, while parallel multiplier, ALU, barrel shifter, register files, and shadow registers support one-cycle multiply-accumulate loops and low-latency interrupts. [Chapter 28, Architecture of the Digital Signal Processor]

A 16-bit fixed-point representation offers uniformly spaced values and low device cost; 32-bit IEEE floating point offers vastly greater dynamic range, relative precision, and easier development because scaling, overflow, and underflow require less manual management. [Chapter 28, Fixed versus Floating Point, Fig. 28-6]

Repeated quantization can dominate fixed-point DSP. The text estimates storage SNR near 30 million-to-one for 32-bit floating point versus about ten-thousand-to-one for 16-bit fixed point, and explains why extended accumulators retain intermediate precision. [Chapter 28, Fixed versus Floating Point]

C improves portability and development speed while assembly exposes maximum hardware parallelism. Efficient DSP C still requires architecture-aware declarations and memory placement; performance must be checked on the actual compiler and target. [Chapter 28, C versus Assembly, Tables 28-2–28-4]

Algorithm throughput is clock rate divided by cycles per sample, not a generic MIPS/MFLOPS headline. On the chapter's 40 MHz SHARC example, conventional FIR throughput spans roughly 100 thousand to 1.6 million samples/s, IIR about 1.8–3.1 million, and FFT routines about 1.8–3.3 million. [Chapter 28, How Fast Are DSPs?, Fig. 28-11]

For the worked 512-sample overlap-add configuration, FFT convolution costs about 60 cycles/sample; this makes direct convolution faster below roughly 60 taps and FFT convolution faster above it, with FFT cost then growing only logarithmically with kernel length. [Chapter 28, How Fast Are DSPs?]

The ADSP-2106x case study emphasizes on-chip memory and I/O bandwidth as first-class design constraints: a 544-kbit SRAM holds about 6–8 seconds of 8-kHz, 8-bit speech, while 4 Mbits can hold a 512×512 8-bit image. [Chapter 29, The ADSP-2106x Family, Table 29-1]

The EZ-KIT workflow treats samples one at a time: a codec interrupt acquires fixed-point input, converts it to floating point, updates a circular delay line, performs a 301-tap parallel multiply-accumulate loop, converts back to fixed point, and returns the output to the codec. [Chapter 29, Design Example: An FIR Audio Filter, Table 29-2]

Symmetric FIR kernels produce exact linear phase: the 301-point example has its center at sample 150, hence a fixed delay of 150 samples, or 18.75 ms at 8 kHz. [Chapter 29, Analog Measurements on a DSP System, Figs. 29-2–29-3]

The measured EZ-KIT response follows the designed custom FIR response within measurement error. The text contrasts ordinary bench-instrument accuracy of roughly 0.1–1% with the codec's roughly 0.001% roundoff scale, motivating higher-resolution acquisition for validating a digital implementation. [Chapter 29, Analog Measurements on a DSP System, Fig. 29-4]

Floating-point execution can push implementation error below algorithm-design error; in the 150-tap Blackman-window example, floating-point roundoff is below the window's approximately 0.02% overshoot, whereas fixed-point coefficient quantization becomes the dominant imperfection. [Chapter 29, Another Look at Fixed versus Floating Point, Fig. 29-5]

FIR filters are comparatively insensitive to coefficient roundoff, while IIR feedback can amplify quantization enough to degrade cutoff, attenuation, overshoot, or even stability; this is a central reason to prefer floating point for sensitive recursive designs. [Chapter 29, Another Look at Fixed versus Floating Point, Figs. 29-5–29-6]

A complex number contains two real components and may be represented as a+jb or as magnitude/phase Me^{jθ}; rectangular form is convenient for addition, while polar/exponential form makes multiplication and division become magnitude products/ratios and angle sums/differences. [Chapter 30, The Complex Number System and Polar Notation, Eqs. 30-8–30-14]
Euler's relation e^{jx}=cos(x)+j sin(x) connects rectangular and polar forms and makes complex exponentials the compact language of sinusoidal DSP. [Chapter 30, Polar Notation, Eqs. 30-11–30-12]

Complex substitution is valid only after a physical problem has been shown to preserve the same algebraic structure; placing two arbitrary real quantities into real and imaginary parts does not license arbitrary complex multiplication. [Chapter 30, Using Complex Numbers by Substitution]

A sinusoid A cos(ωt)+B sin(ωt) maps to the complex value A−jB, or equivalently M e^{jφ}; multiplying by a system's complex response applies amplitude scaling and phase shift while automatically tracking sine/cosine cross-terms. [Chapter 30, Complex Representation of Sinusoids and Systems, Fig. 30-4]

For sinusoidal steady state, impedance turns differential component laws into algebra: resistor, capacitor, and inductor impedances are R, 1/(jωC), and jωL, and the phasor relation V=IZ acts as Ohm's law for magnitude and phase. [Chapter 30, Electrical Circuit Analysis, Fig. 30-5]

The RLC notch example obtains a complete frequency response by substituting impedances into an ordinary voltage-divider relation, illustrating why phasor algebra is simpler than solving the coupled differential equations directly. [Chapter 30, Electrical Circuit Analysis, Figs. 30-6–30-7]

Euler's identities express each real sine or cosine as the sum of equal-status positive- and negative-frequency complex exponentials; one-half of each conjugate frequency component is required to synthesize a unit real sinusoid. [Chapter 31, Mathematical Equivalence, Eqs. 31-3–31-4]

The complex DFT maps an N-point complex time sequence to an N-point complex periodic spectrum. Indices 0…N/2 represent nonnegative frequencies and N/2…N−1 represent wrapped negative frequencies. [Chapter 31, The Complex DFT, Eqs. 31-5–31-8]

A unit real cosine produces two complex spectral components of amplitude one-half. DC and Nyquist are self-paired boundary samples, explaining why the real DFT needs special scaling there while the complex DFT does not. [Chapter 31, The Complex DFT]

A real time-domain signal has conjugate-symmetric spectrum: its real spectral part is even and its imaginary part is odd. Conversely, an imaginary time-domain part produces odd-real/even-imaginary spectral symmetry, enabling two real FFTs to be packed into one complex FFT. [Chapter 31, The Complex DFT, Fig. 31-1]

The Fourier family is organized by discrete/continuous and periodic/aperiodic dualities: DFT, DTFT, Fourier series, and Fourier transform. Discreteness in one domain implies periodicity in the other, while continuity implies aperiodicity. [Chapter 31, The Family of Fourier Transforms, Table 31-1]

Each Fourier transform has analysis by correlation and synthesis by weighted sinusoids. Scaling may be placed on either direction; the chapter uses 1/N, 1/T, or 1/(2π) equivalents for complex forms and twice those values for positive-frequency-only real forms. [Chapter 31, The Family of Fourier Transforms, Table 31-1]

The Laplace transform generalizes the complex Fourier transform by correlating a continuous signal with exponentially weighted sinusoids. The imaginary axis σ=0 is exactly the Fourier transform, while other vertical lines use exponential growth or decay. [Chapter 32, The Nature of the s-Domain, Eq. 32-1 and Fig. 32-1]

For differential-equation systems, impulse responses are combinations of exponentials and sinusoids; the Laplace transform represents such a system compactly by poles and zeros rather than by every point of a waveform. [Chapter 32, opening and Strategy of the Laplace Transform]

A zero is a probing exponential-sinusoid that exactly cancels against the impulse response; a pole lies on the boundary where the transform ceases to converge. A stable causal continuous-time system has no poles in the right half of the s-plane. [Chapter 32, Strategy of the Laplace Transform, Figs. 32-4–32-5]

Circuit analysis maps R, L, and C to R, sL, and 1/(sC), derives the transfer function H(s), evaluates H(jω) for frequency response, and uses partial fractions/inverse transforms for the impulse response. The phasor method is the σ=0 subset. [Chapter 32, Analysis of Electric Circuits, Figs. 32-6–32-8]

Pole-zero distance controls the s-plane response: the magnitude at a point is proportional to the product of distances to zeros divided by the product of distances to poles; phase is the corresponding sum of zero angles minus pole angles. [Chapter 32, The Importance of Poles and Zeros, Fig. 32-7]

A Sallen-Key biquad supplies two poles on a circle of radius 1/RC; amplifier gain moves them from the real axis toward the imaginary axis, sharpening and peaking the response until gain 3 places them on the axis and produces oscillation. [Chapter 32, Filter Design in the s-Domain, Eq. 32-4 and Fig. 32-9]

Classic analog low-pass designs have geometric pole-zero signatures: Butterworth poles are equally spaced on a left-half-plane circle, Chebyshev poles lie on a flattened ellipse to trade passband ripple for transition sharpness, and elliptic filters add imaginary-axis zeros to permit ripple in both bands for the sharpest transition. [Chapter 32, Filter Design in the s-Domain, Figs. 32-10–32-11]

The z-transform X(z)=Σx[n]z^{-n} is the discrete counterpart of the Laplace transform. Writing z=re^{jω} makes radius encode exponential growth/decay and angle encode frequency; vertical s-plane lines map to concentric z-plane circles. [Chapter 33, The Nature of the z-Domain, Eq. 33-1 and Figs. 33-1–33-2]

The unit circle r=1 in the z-plane is the discrete-time frequency-response contour. Stable recursive filters have poles inside it; moving conjugate poles toward unit-circle zeros narrows and sharpens a notch while preserving real coefficients. [Chapter 33, The Nature of the z-Domain and Analysis of Recursive Systems, Fig. 33-3]

A recursive difference equation maps directly to a rational transfer function whose numerator roots are zeros and denominator roots are poles. For a biquad, pole and zero radii/angles yield coefficients by simple cosine relations. [Chapter 33, Analysis of Recursive Systems, Eqs. 33-3–33-5]

To assess an implemented recursive filter, driving the actual coefficient realization with an impulse and FFTing the resulting response reveals roundoff-induced instability that merely evaluating ideal H(z) on the unit circle can miss. [Chapter 33, Analysis of Recursive Systems]

Cascade stages multiply transfer functions and parallel stages add them; polynomial coefficient multiplication is convolution, which turns stage composition into a compact coefficient-array algorithm. [Chapter 33, Cascade and Parallel Stages, Fig. 33-4 and Table 33-1]

Recursive spectral inversion subtracts a filter output from the original signal and changes numerator coefficients while retaining denominator coefficients, but unlike linear-phase FIR inversion it often performs poorly because phase prevents clean cancellation. [Chapter 33, Spectral Inversion, Eqs. 33-6–33-7 and Figs. 33-5–33-6]

Changing only numerator coefficients changes gain without moving poles; normalization evaluates the transfer function at z=1 for DC or z=−1 for Nyquist and divides numerator coefficients by that gain. [Chapter 33, Gain Changes]

The Chebyshev-Butterworth design pipeline places analog prototype poles, warps the circle to a Chebyshev ellipse when ripple is requested, applies the bilinear transform to enter the z-plane, performs low-pass frequency and optional high-pass mappings, cascades biquads, and normalizes gain. [Chapter 33, Chebyshev-Butterworth Filter Design, Figs. 33-7–33-8 and Eqs. 33-8–33-14]

Benford's law predicts P(first digit=d)=log10(d+1)−log10(d); thus 1 leads about 30.1% of values and 2 about 17.6%. Compliant datasets are scale invariant under multiplication by a constant. [Chapter 34, Frank Benford's Discovery, Figs. 34-1–34-2]

Homomorphic processing converts a difficult nonlinear-looking problem into a familiar linear system; for multiplication, taking a logarithm converts products into sums, and for Benford analysis the independent variable is moved to a logarithmic number line. [Chapter 34, Homomorphic Processing]

The Ones Scaling Test repeatedly rescales a dataset and records the fraction with leading digit 1. A compliant dataset remains near 0.301 for every scale; using factors of 1.01 makes the result periodic every roughly 232 steps because 1.01^{232}≈10. [Chapter 34, The Ones Scaling Test, Fig. 34-3 and Table 34-1]

On the base-10 log axis, leading-digit extraction is represented by a period-one sampling function. Shift–multiply–integrate makes the Ones Scaling Test the convolution ost(g)=sf(g)*pdf(−g). [Chapter 34, Writing Benford's Law as a Convolution, Eqs. 34-1–34-3 and Fig. 34-4]

Fourier transformation turns that convolution into OST(f)=SF(f)PDF*(f). Because sf(g) is period one, SF(f) is nonzero only at integer frequencies, reducing compliance to a sparse frequency-domain condition. [Chapter 34, Solving in the Frequency Domain, Eq. 34-4 and Fig. 34-5]

Benford's Law Compliance Theorem: a random process in base B follows Benford's law if and only if the Fourier transform of its log-domain PDF is zero at every nonzero integer frequency. [Chapter 34, Solving Mystery #2, printed p. 715]

The logarithmic leading-digit pattern comes from the periodic sampling function, not a hidden pattern in the original numbers: its DC value fixes log10(2)=0.301 for digit 1 and analogous log intervals for the other digits. [Chapter 34, Solving Mystery #1]

For ordinary smooth distributions, broad width on the log axis makes the frequency-domain PDF narrow enough to vanish near f=1, so broad distributions follow Benford better than narrow ones; oscillatory transforms provide an exceptional exact-compliance route. [Chapter 34, Solving Mystery #2 and More on Following Benford's Law, Figs. 34-6–34-7]

For the log-normal example, doubling log-domain 2σ width from 0.5 to 1.0 changes the Ones Scaling Test from a 16–45% swing to less than 1% fluctuation. Products of independent positive random variables naturally approach broad log-normal distributions via the central-limit effect in log space. [Chapter 34, Analysis of the Log-Normal Distribution, Fig. 34-8]
pedagogy: This shard closes the book with three deliberately different teaching modes. Chapters 27–29 are concrete, implementation-first case studies: compression algorithms are walked by hand through small byte strings and image blocks, while the DSP-hardware chapters trace one FIR sample through buffers, buses, assembly, an evaluation board, and an actual bench measurement. Chapters 30–33 then rebuild the mathematical language the earlier book postponed, moving carefully from complex-number geometry to phasors, the complex Fourier family, the s-plane, and finally the z-plane. Smith's signature method is analogy before algebra: complex substitution is a hammer-and-nail maneuver, the Laplace transform is compared with a train passenger versus a conductor who knows the terrain, and poles and zeros are probing waveforms and landscape features. Derivations are constructive and end in implementable equations or BASIC-like code, especially the full Chebyshev/Butterworth recursive-filter pipeline. Chapter 34 is an extended discovery narrative: a surprising dataset becomes a test, then a convolution, then a frequency-domain theorem and a quantitative experiment. There are no conventional end-of-chapter exercises in this range; worked traces, complete programs, numerical estimates, and figure sequences function as the practice. Chapters 27–29 assume earlier convolution, DCT/FFT, filtering, and programming; Chapters 30–33 require increasingly serious algebra, trigonometry, differential/difference equations, and transform fluency; Chapter 34 assumes probability density, convolution, Fourier transforms, and log scales. Hardware prices, processor families, software screens, market forecasts, MPEG descriptions, and patent remarks are historical, so a current course should preserve the architectural reasoning and measurement workflow while replacing product-selection advice and standards details.

gems: A 1990s web-download calculation makes compression tangible: a roughly 600-kbyte photograph over a 33.6-kbps modem takes about 142 seconds uncompressed, 71 seconds after lossless compression, and 12 seconds as a roughly 50-kbyte JPEG. [Chapter 27, Data Compression Strategies, printed p. 482]

The Huffman text histogram finds that more than 96% of a chapter consists of only 31 characters; a simple five-bit/common-character scheme averages 5.32 bits per character for about 1.5:1 compression. [Chapter 27, Huffman Encoding, Fig. 27-2]

The LZW algorithm is traced byte by byte through the phrase 'the/rain/in/Spain/falls/mainly/on/the/plain,' showing exactly when dictionary strings are added and emitted. [Chapter 27, LZW Compression, Table 27-3]

The JPEG eye block remains recognizable with only 15 of 64 DCT coefficients, while the full photograph at 45:1 compression makes each 8×8 block average fewer than 12 stored bits and visibly reveals the grid. [Chapter 27, JPEG, Figs. 27-12 and 27-15]

MPEG is taught as both compression and editing structure: independently coded I-pictures provide random access, P-pictures exploit temporal redundancy, and B-pictures look both backward and forward. [Chapter 27, MPEG, printed p. 502]

The FIR implementation inventory lists fourteen recurring actions and then shows that a DSP can execute loop steps 6–12 in one clock cycle by parallelizing multiply, add, two fetches, pointer updates, and loop control. [Chapter 28, Circular Buffering and Architecture, Table 28-1]

The benchmark warning is memorable: choosing a processor from a single MIPS/MFLOPS number is compared with asking whether a Cadillac or Ferrari is the better car—the answer depends on the job. [Chapter 28, How Fast Are DSPs?]

A 1024-point complex FFT on the historical 40-MHz ADSP-21062 is budgeted at 18,221 cycles (about 0.46 ms), and the chapter converts that marketing-style fact into the reusable metric of 17.8 cycles/sample. [Chapter 28, How Fast Are DSPs?]

The direct-versus-FFT convolution crossover is worked end to end: a 512-sample block, zero-padding to 1024, forward/inverse FFTs, overlap-add, about 60 cycles/sample, and a roughly 60-tap break-even point. [Chapter 28, How Fast Are DSPs?]
A memory-sizing sanity check translates 544 kbits into 6–8 seconds of 8-kHz, 8-bit speech and 4 Mbits into one 512×512 8-bit image. [Chapter 29, The ADSP-2106x Family, Table 29-1]

The 301-tap FIR assembly listing makes architecture visible: two circular memories feed a multiply, prior product is accumulated, and the next pair is fetched—all on one loop line. [Chapter 29, Design Example: An FIR Audio Filter, Table 29-2]

The analog-engineer vignette turns exact linear phase into a surprise: a 301-point symmetric kernel delays every feature by 150 samples, so the oscilloscope appears mis-triggered even though the system is behaving perfectly. [Chapter 29, Analog Measurements on a DSP System]

The measured-response experiment steps a generator from 125 Hz to 10 kHz in 125-Hz increments and finds the hardware points tracking the intentionally irregular theoretical FIR curve within measurement error. [Chapter 29, Fig. 29-4]

The complex-substitution counterexample uses apple prices and orange prices to show why merely packing two real quantities into a+jb does not guarantee that complex multiplication preserves the original physical problem. [Chapter 30, Using Complex Numbers by Substitution]

A sinusoid is followed across three equivalent languages—ordinary amplitude/phase, rectangular cosine/sine coefficients, and one complex number—then through a system whose complex gain halves amplitude and shifts phase by 3π/8. [Chapter 30, Complex Representation of Systems, Fig. 30-4]

The Laplace train analogy distinguishes exhaustive samples from causal structure: the passenger records every elevation, while the conductor summarizes the route as a mountain, valley, and overall rise—like poles and zeros compressing a full response. [Chapter 32, Strategy of the Laplace Transform]

Five probe waveforms against one notch-filter impulse response turn abstract poles, zeros, and region of convergence into cancellation, finite area, and runaway area. [Chapter 32, Strategy of the Laplace Transform, Fig. 32-5]

The Sallen-Key gain sweep is a compact stability drama: gain 1 yields two real poles, 1.586 places them at 45 degrees, 2.5 produces peaking, and gain 3 reaches the imaginary axis and turns the filter into an oscillator. [Chapter 32, Filter Design in the s-Domain, Fig. 32-9]

The z-plane is explained by an ant walking the unit circle and evaluating H(z) at about 1000 points; the text then undercuts the ideal plot by warning that implemented coefficients can still be unstable, motivating impulse-and-FFT verification. [Chapter 33, Analysis of Recursive Systems]

Recursive spectral inversion is a useful failure case: subtracting a sixth-order Butterworth low-pass from the input produces a terrible high-pass because phase blocks cancellation, whereas notch-to-band-pass inversion fares somewhat better. [Chapter 33, Spectral Inversion, Fig. 33-6]

Benford's origin story begins with the visibly worn first pages of logarithm tables and expands to more than 20,000 values collected from atomic weights, magazine numbers, baseball statistics, and river areas. [Chapter 34, Frank Benford's Discovery]

The empirical confrontation uses 14,414 corporate-tax values against a Gaussian RNG: the tax data show 30.1% leading ones while the RNG does not, immediately posing both the law and its exceptions. [Chapter 34, Fig. 34-2]

The Ones Scaling Test runs 696 multiplications by 1.01, spanning about three orders of magnitude, and repeats every 232 steps because multiplying by ten preserves the leading digit. [Chapter 34, The Ones Scaling Test, Fig. 34-3 and Table 34-1]

A sharp quantitative transition makes the mystery memorable: changing a log-normal distribution's 2σ width from 0.5 to 1.0 changes the predicted leading-one swing from 16–45% to under 1%. [Chapter 34, Analysis of the Log-Normal Distribution, Fig. 34-8]

The book estimates that a log-normal with σ=3 misses exact Benford compliance by such a tiny finite amount that even a billion computers generating a billion numbers per second since the universe began could not statistically expose it. [Chapter 34, Analysis of the Log-Normal Distribution, printed p. 720]

The final application closes the loop from theory to practice: fabricated financial numbers are unlikely to preserve the broad log-domain structure, so leading-digit deviations can flag reports for forensic scrutiny. [Chapter 34, The Power of Signal Processing]
